extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers, faculty, graduate students) and journal editors/publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and policy advice for mathematicians on sharing papers, maintaining profiles, running/participating in online seminars, and how to formulate, test, prove, or disprove conjectures; plus guidance for journals and prize committees about evaluating proofs/disproofs and special issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make papers freely available online
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should put all their papers freely available online (on arXiv or personal website); publishers are generally ok with authors posting their own papers but not with others posting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do this ASAP (even for papers accessible only via subscription). Don't rely on others to host your papers — responsibility is on authors/coauthors. Example: many authors (Noga Alon, Richard Stanley) have hundreds of papers online. If you encounter inaccessible references, email the author asking for a copy. Anti-pattern: assuming library subscriptions will provide wide access (many libraries unsubscribe from major publishers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to use MathSciNet and Zentralblatt
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should learn to use professional bibliographic databases like MathSciNet and Zentralblatt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with these databases aids literature search and referencing; treat them as essential research tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a comprehensive personal website and Google Scholar profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your website updated with papers, slides, video links and ensure your Google Scholar profile is cleaned up and current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly remove incorrect/duplicate items and non-research files from Google Scholar; add slides/videos to help people working remotely. Small maintenance takes minutes but influences how others judge you; unattended profiles can get overrun with irrelevant items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep rights to display public copies when signing book contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: When signing a book contract, retain the right to display a public copy on your website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be considerate of online readers; ensuring the right to host a chapter or section can aid teaching and access. Anti-pattern: refusing to share short sections leading to loss of community goodwill and reduced educational impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in good home computing and teaching infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain adequate home computing, cameras, lights, whiteboards, and other equipment to support online seminars/teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use downtime (holidays) to reflect on what worked and improve setup; while investments may be deferred due to uncertainty, quality home setups materially affect online research/teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read evaluations and act on feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully read teaching/research evaluations and make changes when problems are identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if departments don't compensate for extra work, responding to evaluations is a small price for job security and improved performance; take constructive criticism seriously and implement practical fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and invite junior colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Established researchers should actively support junior colleagues by inviting them to give talks, helping with papers and applications, and replying to emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a winner-take-all online era juniors are easily overlooked; small actions (invites, feedback, replies) can materially help their careers. Anti-pattern: repeatedly inviting only well-known mathematicians and ignoring juniors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize local online events and seminars
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize and run locally focused online seminars, workshops, and conferences to sustain community interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite many global online events, local online efforts are important to preserve community ties and help shy or shell-shocked colleagues engage; such events can be critical until in-person activity resumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal evaluation criterion — problem importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the problem being solved old, famous, or well-studied?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider the prominence and historical interest of the problem when evaluating submissions resolving open problems; high prominence increases publication likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal evaluation criterion — novelty/interest of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the tools and methods used in the solution interesting or innovative enough to be helpful in future studies?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers employing new or broadly useful techniques score higher on this criterion; purely ad hoc or unilluminating methods are less valued even if they resolve a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal evaluation criterion — significance of implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the implications of the solution for other problems and areas justify publication?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors evaluate whether the solution has meaningful consequences elsewhere; broad impact raises the paper's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should publish computational and experimental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should be open to publishing computational/experimental studies, computational confirmations of conjectures, and rigorous computational disproofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to accept computational evidence, heuristics, and algorithmic/experimental contributions as legitimate research; examples include acceptance (after controversy) of large computational proofs (Kepler) and the value of computational searches for counterexamples (e.g., testing Lovász conjecture instances). Anti-pattern: rejecting computational disproofs or experimental studies out of hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize and institution policy — award all valid progress (proofs/disproofs/independence) fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize rules and institutions should be neutral to whether the outcome is a proof, disproof, or independence result, and should allow flexible/partial awards evaluated by independent committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wording that rewards only proofs; set independent scientific committees to allocate funds for proofs, disproofs, independence results, or substantial partial progress. Example guidance: allow partial awards for substantial partial results (e.g., huge bounds covering most cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a conjecture interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjecture is typically deemed interesting if it is sharply formulated, has deep roots, wide ramifications, or implies many notable consequences (a feeling of unity), but this is subjective and potentially self-referential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: many consequences could indicate a conjecture is too strong (and thus likely false). The value of a conjecture includes how well it guides research and inspires work; 'feeling of unity' is not an objective standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a conjecture believable (evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures are believed if they hold in special cases and imply other conjectures or known results that are themselves believed (testing special cases and understanding consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize circularity: using other conjectures as evidence can be self-referential. Prefer independent checks: computational tests in many small cases and implications that are plausibly necessary rather than merely convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to pursue disproofs of conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Disproving conjectures can be (1) opportunistic (niches exist because most try to prove), (2) beautiful (constructing counterexamples can reveal surprising diversity), and (3) constructive (requires building explicit counterexamples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disproof work is valuable: it opens research directions, can be computationally intensive, and often leads to new constructions and insights. Treat disproofs as research of equal intrinsic value to proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make conjectures explicit in papers
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing papers, explicitly state conjectures (what you wanted to prove but couldn't) so others may work on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating conjectures helps guide young researchers and potential collaborators; don't fear being wrong — the conjecture may still be useful even if false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check conjectures computationally in many small cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Before asserting confidence, test conjectures computationally across many small cases to provide supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental verification in many small instances increases credibility and helps others take conjectures seriously; computational effort can be indispensable when small counterexamples do not exist and brute-force is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computational experiments to explore and formulate conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate and refine conjectures via computational experiments and exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation often leads to new conjectures and insights; journals should recognize experimental and computational contributions as valid scholarly work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand your abilities and seek collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess your own skills, tools, and limitations when approaching a conjecture and look for collaborators with complementary expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborators may have different perspectives and technical toolkits that help decide whether to attempt proof or disproof and how to attack a problem; actively seek such partnerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brave and optimistic in proposing or attacking conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether aiming to prove, disprove, or state new conjectures, adopt a brave and optimistic attitude and ignore unconstructive criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persist in stating and tackling conjectures despite potential negative judgments from prominent figures; constructive risk-taking can lead to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of guest special-issue publishing pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Special/guest issues can devolve into low-quality or nepotistic volumes where guest editors solicit and accept many submissions with social pressure to accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should resist undue social pressure, maintain independent standards, and avoid automatic acceptance of invited papers. Publishers and editors must ensure scientific oversight; anti-patterns include using guest issues to pad CVs, honorific volumes with little editorial scrutiny, and recycling paper copies that nobody reads.
